Definition
This lesson introduces the student to the principles of troubleshooting closed loop feedback systems.
INTRODUCTIONM

There are many different methods of controlling motors by using feedback. No matter how complicated the feedback system may appear, a systematic troubleshooting approach will always yield satisfactory results...
Troubleshooting is a diverse process that involves theoretical knowledge, test equipment competency, and an understanding of equipment operation, all blended together with a little intuition.

A particular symptom may be caused by any number of reasons, many of which will not seem logical. Therefore, the best troubleshooters are those who can exercise both logical and creative thought processes...

DISCUSSION
The experienced troubleshooter knows that many factors come into play when trying to solve a system fault, and will not be shocked that a suspected component is not actually the problem.

The troubleshooting process has been and will continue to be defined in several different ways. Different organizations may use different terminology and divide the process into a different number of phases. The following terms can be used for the first phase of the troubleshooting process: Setup check * Functional test * Circuit analysisssss

Technicians will be exposed to many terms and number of varying troubleshooting phases. No single recipe for troubleshooting exists; only time and practice and adherence to tried and proven guidelines will structure your way of thinking...
As with any service-related work, customer satisfaction is the goal. Quality work and quick turn-around time are the keys to that goal.
Before diving into an equipment failure, the technician should fully analyze all the possible symptoms. The troubleshooting process consists of four basic steps:

During the assessment process, the technician should evaluate: What is the equipment doing? What is the equipment not doing? When an initial assessment is done properly, some problems can be identified without the need for in-depth troubleshooting.ng.

A good visual inspection can help identify obvious conditions, such as unplugged power cords, burned out light bulbs, blown fuses and controls set to the wrong position. When identifying a fault, localization may require either signal injection or signal tracing or both....

Most equipment today, contains either a Built in Test (BIT), or a computerized diagnostic operational test to help the technician localize the problem to a section, stage or even to the component level. Once the stage or component is isolated, the technician can make the required repairs...

After replacing or repairing the failed component, the technician should run an operational check to re-assess the proper functioning of the equipment. This verifies the repair, and makes sure no new problems were created during the maintenance procedure.

The process of signal tracing through a system involves methodically observing a signal along the signal path. This signal can be derived from an internal source or generated by test equipment. The best overall approach is to use the back-to-front method that is tracing the output signal backwards toward the source.....

An alternative method of signal tracing is to pick a point somewhere in the middle of the signal path and check there first. If the signal is present work towards the output and if the signal is not present work backwards towards the input...

Some input signals are excessively small for detection by an oscilloscope. If your signal tracing efforts have brought you to this point, you will need to use a function or signal generator in order to isolate the problem...

Signal injection is the process of applying a generated signal of appropriate frequency either to the input or to some point along the signal path. If, for example, the Pulse Width Modulator (PWM) clock stage is known to be faulty; you could inject a minimum level 70 Hz, 2Vpp square wave directly to the input of the PWM stage.....

However, when injecting into the PWM's signal path, keep the injected signal's amplitude at minimum and slowly raise it until the signal can start and stop the motor by using the MOTOR SPEED control on the Model 170 Trainer. Too large a signal can destroy the PWM...

Another signal injection example is to simulate the square wave signal from the speed detector. Inserting a minimum level 100 Hz to 700 Hz, 4 Vpp square wave directly to the input or output of the wave shaper will simulate the speed detector output...

Remember, when troubleshooting a closed loop feedback DC motor system, the output of the device (motor) has a direct effect on the input back to that same device. The output of the motor (by use of the speed detector) dictates the input to the same motor...

The first concept a troubleshooter should perform is to separate the system into stages. Stage isolation allows the technician to step logically through the system without having to check each individual component...

Utilizing a block diagram can help the technician isolate the system into stages. Notice, that a system that routes a feedback signal back to the controlling circuits is what composes a closed loop system...
Secondly, the troubleshooter should group the stages into major sections. In our discussion, we will use two major sections:
* CONTROL CIRCUITRY
The SENSING circuitry section consists of the speed detector, frequency to voltage (F/V) converter, Proportional Integral Derivative (PID) controller, speed reference, and error detector stages...
The CONTROL circuitry section consists of the PWM controller and the H-switch/driver stages.(

The following steps will be utilized when troubleshooting the closed loop motor feedback system in the Nida Model 170 Trainer.
Perform a visual inspection to verify the equipment is set up properly.
Verify that the problem is not related to the motor itself.
Verify there is an input to the control circuits from the sensing circuits.
Verify there is output from the control circuits to the motor.

The speed detector senses the motor's RPMs by the use of a disk mounted on the motor's shaft. As the disk rotates on the spinning shaft, the outside edge of the disk passes between and LED and a phototransistor...

The disk has a series of holes that allows the light generated by the LED to periodically pass through the disk and into the phototransistor. Each time the light passes through the disk, the phototransistor develops a positive pulse...

The number of pulses generated during a given amount of time determines the motor's speed. The end result is a string (train) of positive pulses that is sent to the frequency-to-voltage (F/V) converter (U4B on PC130-179)...
U4B and U5 on PC130-179 comprise the major components of the frequency-to-voltage (F/V) converter. Wave shaper U4B receives square waves from the speed detector (TP6 on
PC130-179) and modifies the square waves to form clean leading edges.
U5 transforms the pulse train into a voltage. This voltage (TP5 on PC130-179) is variable depending on the frequency of the pulse train and is the input to the PID circuits.
The PID controller is a rapid acting and corrective controller. The proportional, integral and derivative controller demonstrates the means to maintain a desired actuator (motor) position control.
The PID controller is operating properly when the output of the controller has a fast rise time, low overshoot, correct gain, and reaches the set point value.

The PID circuit uses a series of operational amplifiers to reshape the error signal. The proportional and derivative circuits consist of one operational amplifier. The integral circuit consists of two operational amplifiers. U1 and U2 on the PC130-177 comprise the PID and pass the output to the error detector...

The MOTOR SPEED control (R1) on the Model 170 Trainer is the major component of the speed reference circuit. This variable resistor picks off a voltage from 0 VDC to +5 VDC and is the comparison voltage input to the error detector...
U1 on PC130-178 is the error detection circuit. The two comparison inputs to the error detector come from the PID circuit at (TP1 on PC130-178) and the MOTOR SPEED (R1) speed reference...
When the inputs are compared and a difference voltage is present, the detector circuit produces an error voltage, which is sent to the PWM controller at (TP2 on PC130-178).

The Pulse Width Modulator (PWM) circuit consists of U2 and U3 on PC130-178. U3 generates the clock signal used by U2 at (TP4 on PC130-178). U2 (the PWM) modulates the pulse width from the clock with the voltage input from the error detector at (TP2
on PC130-178) and sends it to the H-switch/driver at (TP3 on

U3 and S2 on PC130-179 make up the H-switch/driver. This section controls the direction of the DC motor and provides sufficient current to drive the motor. S2 selects the voltage inputs to U3 for the motor direction (CW/CCW) control...

The H-switch/driver amplifies the signal from the PWM controller at (TP3 on PC130-178) and sends it to the motor at (TP2 on PC130-179). The motor receives the PWM signal from the H-switch/driver through S1 (ON) and S2 (OUT). The amplified PWM signal can be monitored between TJ3 and TJ4 on the Model 170 Trainer.....
